title: Cross-National Insights into Anxiety Symptoms Among Young Adults in South Africa, Namibia, and Kenya
abstract: Sub-Saharan Africa has the fastest-growing population of adolescents and young adults globally, comprising approximately 23% of the population. Young adults face social, economic, and developmental transitions that may increase vulnerability to anxiety disorders. Prevalence estimates for anxiety across the region, including South Africa, Namibia, and Kenya, ranging from 11% to 20%. This cross-sectional study examined anxiety symptoms among 2,460 young adults (18–19 years) from South Africa, Namibia, and Kenya. Measurement invariance was established. Within- and between-country comparisons were conducted across gender, socioeconomic status (SES), and religiosity using ANOVAs, and correlations. South African participants reported higher anxiety than those in Namibia and Kenya. Females and individuals with lower perceived SES reported higher anxiety, while religious involvement showed a modest protective association. Findings highlight the importance of culturally and socioeconomically informed mental health strategies for emerging adults in diverse African contexts.
